properties.decision:
RULED 2026-09-13 by @ajs: YES, NARROWLY — an in-memory design is reachable at launch, as `--ephemeral`, and is presented as a SCRATCH MODE rather than as a storage choice. Built the same day.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT CHANGED ABOUT THE QUESTION. flo2's restatement described this as a feature request needing a runtime selector. Reading the source first showed the work was far smaller and the risk far more specific:
 · the in-memory engine EXISTS and is not experimental — several hundred tests run against it
 · `ReflowService::in_memory()` already existed
 · the server binary already compiles with no store (`cargo check -p reflow2-mcp --no-default-features` passes)
 · `main.rs` referenced `in_memory` ZERO times — the only missing piece was a way to ASK

So this was never "build a second engine". It was "reach one that is already there", and the decision turned on product shape rather than on effort.

⭐ WHY NOT A NEUTRAL `--backend memory`. That name frames durability as a preference between two equal options, and for this product it is not one: reflow2's whole premise is that a design outlives the session. The flag is named for WHAT HAPPENS TO YOUR WORK, not for which engine is underneath. A flag that quietly turns off the memory is a foot-gun pointed at the one thing the tool is for.

HOW THE FOOT-GUN IS BLUNTED, and each of these is a refusal rather than a warning:
 · `--graph-path`, `--registry-root`, `--shared` and `--serve-shared` are all REFUSED alongside it — every one of them names a design on disk, and the combination is far likelier to be a mistake than an intention. Detected from the ARGUMENTS for `--graph-path`, because a parsed value cannot tell "the user asked for this" from "clap filled in the default".
 · The handshake says it FIRST, before anything else, because an agent connecting over HTTP never sees the operator's stderr banner. The condition is `graph_path: None` — the same fact rather than a second flag that could drift from it — and `share()` copies it, so every per-session service carries the warning.
 · `--export-to` still works, so a scratch design can be written through after all.

TWO EARLIER RULINGS POINT THE SAME WAY AND NEITHER IS CONTRADICTED. `dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds` (REJECTED 2026-09-11) and `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability` (RULED 2026-09-11, the store STAYS) are both about REPLACING the engine. This is about REACHING one that ships, for measurement and scratch work, and RocksDB remains the only way a design persists.

HOW FLO2 GETS WHAT IT ASKED FOR: start `--ephemeral`, then load a real design with the `import_graph` tool, and measure that against the same design on the store. Their open question is answerable without a second binary and without anybody patching main.rs.

WHAT IS NOT SETTLED HERE: whether an ephemeral design should ever be reachable in a hosted deployment. The refusals keep it away from `--registry-root` today, which is the conservative reading; if a hosted scratch tier is ever wanted, that is a new question and this ruling does not answer it.
properties.name: OPEN — is the byte backend selectable at RUNTIME, or does choosing it stay a compile-time act?
properties.rationale:
Ruled after checking the three facts the answer depended on rather than accepting the framing: the in-memory engine exists and is exercised by several hundred tests, the server binary builds with no store at all, and main.rs never reaches the constructor. That turned "should we build a selector" into "should we expose one that is already built", and the honest answer to a consumer asking a fair question was yes.

The narrowing is where the judgement is. A full runtime backend selector would present durability as a configuration preference; `--ephemeral` presents throwing your work away as a deliberate, awkward, clearly-labelled act, and refuses every flag that names a design on disk.
